title: One Rock, Many Causes
paragraphs: Questions about mass extinction invite a single culprit, and the end of the non-bird dinosaurs sixty-six million years ago has long been pinned on an asteroid. The evidence for the impact is strong, with the crater centred on the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico, yet the question of how an impact translates into a global extinction is considerably more delicate.

The Natural History Museum in London treats the asteroid as the final blow, not the sole cause. Its account stresses that the last dinosaurs lived in an already changing world, some of whose environmental shifts began millions of years before the collision. On this view, a stressed ecosystem was pushed past its limit by a catastrophe it might have survived in better health.

Other experts locate the decisive mechanism elsewhere. An article from the United States National Science Foundation argues that the climate changes following the impact, rather than the blast itself, most likely caused the mass death. An international panel, reporting in twenty ten, concluded by contrast that the impact best explains the extinction, while the American Museum of Natural History notes that some paleontologists think dinosaurs were already declining beforehand. Such disagreements are less a sign of confusion than of a field still refining its causal story.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that nothing survived. Birds descend from one branch of the theropod dinosaurs, and the lineages that led to them came through the catastrophe. The extinction was therefore selective, removing some large animals entirely while leaving others to flourish.

What the debate ultimately teaches is humility. The wiser course is to hold each explanation loosely while the measurements continue and new data arrive. A neat story of one rock and one bad day is satisfying, but the evidence points to a tangled chain of stress, impact and aftermath, and we understand the past best when we accept that complexity.
